Business plan text:

Inhalerbuddy
Executive Summary: Inhalerbuddy LLC
Overview
Inhalerbuddy is a connected health startup that is passionate about changing the way that
families, schools and pharmacies think about childhood asthma. We are a team of three students
at our university and we have formed an LLC and built a working prototype. This executive
summary will describe the problem, our solution, the market, our business model, the
competition, our team, our milestones and what we are asking for.
The Problem
Asthma is a very common condition among children and it is a problem that effects millions of
families. Many kids with asthma do not take there medicine the way that the doctor said, and
parents often do not know when a inhaler was used or not used. Sometimes a child will use the
rescue inhaler a lot more then normal in the days before a attack, but nobody notices because
there is no good way to see the pattern. This can lead to emergency room visits, missed school
days, and stress for the whole family. We beleive that this is a big problem that is not being
solved well today and that technology can help. Parents are busy and they want peace of mind
about there child's health.
The Solution
Our solution is Inhalerbuddy, which is a end-to-end platform that leverages Internet of Things
sensing, mobile software and human pharmacist support to create a seamless asthma management
experience. It has three pieces.
First, the Inhalerbuddy cap. This is a small electronic cap that snaps on to the top of most
common inhalers. It has a sensor that detects when the inhaler is pressed and it sends the time
to the phone using wireless. The cap is lightweight and designed to be kid friendly with fun
colors.
Second, the Inhalerbuddy app. The app shows caregivers a dashboard of when the medicine was
used. If the rescue inhaler is used more often then usual, the app sends a alert to the
caregivers so they can check on the child, call the doctor or take other steps before symptoms
get worse. The app also has reminders for daily controller medicine.
Third, the pharmacist check-in service. Once in a while a pharmacist reviews the data and
checks in with the family by message or call to answer questions and make sure the child is
using the inhaler properly. We think this human touch is what makes us different and gives
parents trust.
Together these three pieces create a holistic solution that is proactive instead of reactive.
Market
The market for our product is very large. There are millions of children with asthma in the
United States alone and the market for digital health is growing very fast. If we capture even
a small percent of families with asthmatic children, this would be a very large business. We
also believe there are opportunities internationally and with other conditions besides asthma,
such as other respiratory conditions and chronic disease management. Our target customers are
parents of children with asthma, and secondarily schools, pediatricians and pharmacies. We have
not yet done a formal market study but we have talked to a few parents and friends who thought
the idea was good.
Business Model
We plan to make money in several ways, and we are still figuring out which will work best. One

option is to sell the cap as a one time purchase to parents at a price of around thirty to
fifty dollars. Another option is a monthly subscription for the app and the pharmacist service,
maybe five to ten dollars a month. We could also partner with pharmacies, insurance companies
or health systems who might pay us to offer Inhalerbuddy to their patients or members. There is
also the possibility of selling anonymized data to researchers or pharmaceutical companies,
which could be very valuable. We think a mix of these revenue streams will make the business
sustainable. Pricing will be determined after we do more testing with customers.
Competition
There are some other companies that make smart inhaler sensors and asthma apps. However we feel
that our product is better because it combines hardware, software and a pharmacist service in
one package and because it is focused on kids and caregivers. Other products are mostly for
adults or for the patient only. Also, our design is more fun and friendly for children. We
believe that no competitor offers the full solution that we do, and we have a first mover
advantage in the pharmacist check-in piece. We will also build a strong brand which will be
hard to copy.
Team
Brandon Tilley is our CEO and he is a junior studying business. He is a natural leader and has
always been interested in health and entrepreneurship. Marisol Quenneville is our CTO and she
is a senior studying electrical engineering, and she designed and built the prototype cap.
Devraj Ostrowski is our head of product and he is a junior studying computer science, and he
built the first version of the app. Our team is hardworking, passionate and committed to making
Inhalerbuddy a success. We do not yet have a pharmacist or a clinician on the team but we plan
to find advisors, and one of our relatives is a nurse who has given us some feedback.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two main milestones. We defined our core business concept and we built a
prototype of the cap and a early version of the app. We have also formed a LLC. The prototype
works in the lab and can detect when it is pressed and send the data to the phone, although the
battery life and the fit on different inhalers still needs work. We have not yet tested with
real patients or children and we have no customers or revenue at this time. We have also not
yet made a website. Our expenses so far have been small and paid for by the founders out of
pocket, mostly for electronic parts and a few app tools. Over the next year, we expect to need
money for manufacturing, regulatory work, app development, pharmacist staffing and marketing.
We think we could reach substantial revenue in about three years if things go well, though we
have not yet built a detailed financial model.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for several reasons. First, we hope to win prize money
which we would use to improve the prototype and begin a small pilot. Second, we are looking for
mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs and healthcare professionals who can help us with our
business model and with navigating regulations. Third, we would like introductions to potential
partners such as pharmacies, pediatric clinics and schools. Finally we want feedback from the
judges on how to make our idea stronger. We are excited about the opportunity and we thank you
for considering our application. With your support we beleive Inhalerbuddy can make a real
difference in the lives of children with asthma and there families.

Question: What can the team do to improve their written submission?

response.text:
The team can improve their written submission by:

1. **Clarifying the Problem Statement**: The problem is described in a general way. They should quantify the issue (e.g., how many children are affected, how often non-compliance leads to ER visits) and clearly define the gap in current solutions.

2. **Defining the Target Market**: They need to specify the exact target audience (e.g., age range, geographic location, socioeconomic factors) and provide data or estimates on market size and potential customer base.

3. **Strengthening the Business Model**: They should outline a clear, data-backed pricing strategy and revenue model, including customer acquisition costs, lifetime value, and scalability.

4. **Enhancing the Competitive Analysis**: They should provide specific examples of competitors, their features, pricing, and market share, and clearly articulate how Inhalerbuddy differentiates itself.

5. **Adding Financial Projections**: They should include a basic financial model with revenue, expenses, and break-even analysis, even if preliminary.

6. **Improving the Executive Summary Structure**: The summary should be more concise, with clear sections (problem, solution, market, business model, etc.) and a compelling value proposition.

7. **Adding Customer Validation**: They should include feedback from potential customers (e.g., parents, pediatricians) to demonstrate market interest and validate the problem-solution fit.

8. **Specifying Regulatory Requirements**: They should identify relevant regulations (e.g., FDA, HIPAA) and outline how they plan to comply, which is critical for a health-related product.

9. **Improving Grammar and Tone**: The submission contains grammatical errors and informal language (e.g., "we beleive," "there is no good way to see the pattern"). A more polished, professional tone is needed.

10. **Including a Go-to-Market Strategy**: They should outline how they plan to launch the product, including marketing channels, partnerships, and distribution strategies.
